result.question: How can Apple Silicon (M3 Max) GPU and Neural Engine actually be utilized for training and real-time inference of warping-based neural-head-avatar models (TPS / grid_sample / FOMM / MobilePortrait), given that PyTorch MPS lacks grid_sampler_2d_backward and falls back to CPU? Cover: (1) MLX — does it have grid_sample forward+backward? custom Metal kernels via mx.fast.metal_kernel? autograd support for custom kernels? (2) writing a custom Metal grid_sample backward and registering it for PyTorch MPS; (3) CoreML/ANE (Neural Engine) for inference of conv+warp models and what ops the ANE supports/excludes; (4) which path is most practical to actually get real GPU compute (not CPU fallback) for this warping architecture on an M3 Max. Then recommend something concrete to build.
result.summary: Yes — real Apple Silicon GPU compute for warping-based head-avatar models (TPS/grid_sample/FOMM/MobilePortrait) is achievable today, and the clear winner is MLX, not PyTorch MPS or CoreML/ANE. MLX provides a complete, documented, differentiable grid_sample built with mx.fast.metal_kernel (a JIT-compiled custom Metal kernel) wrapped in mx.custom_function with a hand-written @.vjp backward — so BOTH forward and backward warping run on the M3 Max GPU (no CPU fallback), reaching ~8x forward and ~40x backward speedups over composable-op implementations on an M1 Max. This is exactly the gap PyTorch MPS leaves open: grid_sampler_2d falls back to CPU and grid_sampler_2d_backward is unimplemented (issue #97606, still open), and PyTorch's own Metal-kernel tutorial (mps_custom_ops.html) is now a 404 with no live substitute documenting an MPS grid_sample backward. For inference-only deployment, CoreML can convert grid_sample to the MIL 'resample'/'affine' op and run on GPU (and intermittently the ANE), but ANE placement is OS-controlled and historically fragile, making it a secondary path. Concrete recommendation: build the warping core of MobilePortrait in pure MLX, porting Apple's canonical grid_sample forward+VJP Metal kernels from the MLX docs/barronalex gist directly into /root/mobileportrait-mlx — this is the only path that gives real GPU compute for both training and real-time inference of this architecture on an M3 Max.

findings.claim: MLX is the most practical path: it has working JIT-compiled Metal GPU kernels for grid_sample AND its gradient (via mx.fast.metal_kernel + mx.custom_function/@.vjp), so both forward and backward warping run on the Apple GPU with no CPU fallback.
findings.evidence: MLX core dev barronalex: 'we now have fast GPU kernels for grid_sample and its gradient! They're written with mx.fast.metal_kernel.' The gist contains a forward Metal kernel, a SEPARATE grid_sample_grad kernel (atomic_outputs=True), and @mx.custom_function + @grid_sample.vjp autograd wiring, matching torch.nn.functional.grid_sample defaults. The official MLX docs use grid_sample as the canonical worked example and state 'We can now use mx.grad and the gradients will be computed using our custom Metal kernels' — i.e., backward warping runs on the GPU, not CPU. Before the kernel, a pure-MLX gather-based version was also made differentiable (PR #1256 added zero VJPs for gather-w.r.t-indices and bitwise ops), matching PyTorch outputs/gradients for bilinear/zeros. Caveat: the kernels live in a gist/docs example, not a built-in mlx.core op, so you port them rather than import them.

findings.claim: MLX's custom-kernel + autograd stack is first-class and fully documented: mx.fast.metal_kernel JIT-compiles a Metal kernel body (signature auto-generated, cached after first run); kernels are non-differentiable by default (throw on grad) but become differentiable by wrapping in mx.custom_function and defining the backward via the @.vjp decorator, which then participates in mx.grad/value_and_grad.
findings.evidence: Docs: 'MLX supports writing custom Metal kernels through the Python and C++ APIs... Only the kernel body is required, the function signature is generated automatically... MLX will compile the kernel the first time it is run and cache it.' And: 'The above will throw an error since there are no gradients defined for our custom kernel. To make our kernel differentiable we wrap it in a custom_function and define the gradient transformations.' custom_function docs confirm @f.vjp registers a reverse-mode gradient used by value_and_grad(). PR #1325 ('Custom Metal Kernels from Python', barronalex, merged ~Aug 22 2024) introduced mx.fast.metal_kernel with auto-generated signatures from input/output shapes+dtypes. Note: the custom_function doc page itself does not mention grid_sample/Metal — that integration is documented separately in the custom_metal_kernels guide.

findings.claim: PyTorch MPS genuinely lacks a usable warping path: grid_sampler_2d falls back to CPU even on macOS versions the warning claims support it, the warning is misleading, and grid_sampler_2d_backward is not implemented — so training warping models on MPS hits CPU fallback.
findings.evidence: Reporter on macOS 13.3: 'grid_sampler_2d op is falling back to CPU, but is supported natively on MPS with macOS >=13.1... Either the warning is wrong about what versions it is supported on, or the compatibility check is not working correctly.' Issue is still OPEN (not fixed); labeled triaged/module:mps. Forward got partial MPS support but backward (grid_sampler_2d_backward) was not implemented, reinforcing the fallback problem for training. A competing claim that torch 2.5.1 resolved it was REFUTED 1-2.

findings.claim: Writing a custom Metal grid_sample backward for PyTorch MPS is technically possible but currently the worst-documented path: the dedicated tutorial (mps_custom_ops.html) is a 404, the closest live substitute (cpp_custom_ops.html) covers only C++/CUDA with zero mention of MPS/Metal/grid_sample, though the substrate exists (in-tree MetalShaderLibrary compiles MSL to a pipeline state) and the autograd.Function/setup_context+backward contract is the wiring mechanism.
findings.evidence: mps_custom_ops.html returns HTTP 404 ('Page Not Found'); cpp_custom_ops.html: 'This tutorial provides a basic introduction to creating a custom operator (custom op) in C++ and CUDA' — no MPS/Metal/grid_sample. PyTorch PR #125550 introduced/factored the in-tree C++ MetalShaderLibrary that compiles MSL SHADER_SOURCE and produces an MTLComputePipelineState — the substrate a custom MPS grid_sample backward would use. The autograd contract is documented: forward() must not take ctx; setup_context(ctx, inputs, output) saves tensors; backward receives one grad per output and returns one grad per input (None for non-diff). Net: doable but you'd be writing both the Metal kernel and the autograd glue with no official grid_sample-on-MPS guide — far more effort than MLX, which ships the exact kernels.

findings.claim: For inference-only deployment, PyTorch grid_sampler IS convertible to CoreML — coremltools' torch frontend maps it to the MIL 'resample' op (direct grid coords) or 'affine' op (from affine_grid_generator) — so warp models can run on CoreML GPU at inference despite the MPS training gap; this is a viable secondary/deployment path.
findings.evidence: coremltools ops.py has @register_torch_op handlers for affine_grid_generator and grid_sampler; the latter emits mb.resample(coordinates_mode='normalized_minus_one_to_one') for direct coords, or mb.affine(...) when from affine_grid_generator. CoreML conversion is a forward-only graph-translation path entirely separate from PyTorch's MPS backward kernels, so the missing grid_sampler_2d_backward does NOT block inference conversion. Caveats: rank-4 only (5D is an open feature request #2284); FP16 conversion shows output discrepancy vs FP32 (#2068); resample commonly lands on GPU rather than ANE.

findings.claim: ANE support for grid_sample/resample is real but OS-gated and fragile, not developer-controllable: it ran on ANE on M2/macOS 14, a macOS 15 beta channel-validation bug pushed it off ANE, and Apple fixed it in macOS 15.1 beta 5 — but ANE placement is decided by OS-level op validation, so you cannot rely on or force ANE execution for a conv+warp graph.
findings.evidence: Reporter (M2): 'macOS 15 beta... PyTorch's gridsample function is not executing on Apple's Neural Engine.' Apple maintainer: 'It's due to the resample op fall off ANE which is caused by some channel validation logic'; 'It's a bug in ANE op validation (not in CoreML)'; closing: 'The fix has been landed in MacOS 15.1 beta 5.' Third party: 'you cannot control whether an operation is executed on ANE or CPU or on GPU.' So ANE for warp ops is possible on current macOS but governed by OS op-validation rules — treat ANE acceleration as a bonus, not a design guarantee; target GPU as the reliable inference accelerator.

findings.claim: Concrete build recommendation: implement the MobilePortrait warping core in pure MLX by porting Apple's grid_sample forward+VJP Metal kernels (MLX docs / barronalex gist) into the existing /root/mobileportrait-mlx repo, replacing the grid_sample calls in src/modules/dense_motion.py, model.py, and inpainting_network.py.
findings.vote: derived from merged MLX findings [5][6][11][12][19][20] (all 3-0 except [5] 2-1) + local repo confirmation in [20]
findings.evidence: Claim [20] verifier confirmed the local repo already uses grid_sample in src/modules/dense_motion.py, model.py, and inpainting_network.py — the exact warping architecture in question. MLX gives a drop-in differentiable GPU grid_sample (forward + atomic VJP backward) matching torch.nn.functional.grid_sample defaults, with ~8x/40x measured speedups (forward/backward) on M1 Max. Building plan: (1) port the forward grid_sample mx.fast.metal_kernel and the grid_sample_grad VJP kernel into an mlx module, wrap with @mx.custom_function/@.vjp; (2) numerically validate against torch.nn.functional.grid_sample (bilinear, padding_mode='zeros', align_corners) on M3 Max; (3) wire it into dense_motion/model/inpainting_network; (4) train and run real-time inference fully on the M3 Max GPU. Keep a CoreML 'resample' export as the optional deployment/inference-distribution path. Caveat: the MLX kernels are docs/gist examples (not a built-in op) and the verified-fast example is bilinear/zeros — other modes/padding need their own kernel variants and validation.

result.caveats: Time-sensitivity / version drift: All MLX evidence is from 2024-era PRs/docs and verifiers note it remains current as of May 2026 (MLX ~0.31.x), but mx.fast.metal_kernel/custom_function are still evolving APIs — re-verify signatures against the installed MLX version before porting. The benchmark numbers (8x forward / 40x backward) are first-party MLX docs on an M1 Max, not M3 Max, and only for mode='bilinear', padding_mode='zeros'; other sampling modes/padding require writing additional kernel variants and re-validating, and a separate claim of ~28x training speedup was REFUTED (0-3), so do not over-rely on a single speedup figure. The MLX grid_sample lives in a core-dev gist and the official docs example, NOT as a built-in mlx.core/mlx.nn op (barronalex called it too specialized to merge) — you must port and maintain it yourself. Split-vote (2-1) claims [0], [4], [14], [21] carry residual uncertainty: [4] is specifically a regression-repair, NOT a guarantee any conv+warp graph runs on ANE; [21]'s ANE portion is its weakest part (resample usually lands on GPU). The CoreML inference path was verified against the converter source code, not by running a converted MobilePortrait model end-to-end. PyTorch's in-tree Metal substrate (PR #125550) was confirmed but a related claim about the user-facing torch.mps.compile_shader API timeline was REFUTED (1-2), so the exact PyTorch public custom-MPS-kernel surface is unsettled. Finally, I could not independently re-read the local repo files this session (filesystem tool calls returned empty); the repo-content grounding (grid_sample in dense_motion.py/model.py/inpainting_network.py) comes from the verified claim [20] rather than a fresh read.
openQuestions: Does the MLX bilinear/zeros grid_sample VJP kernel cover all sampling/padding modes MobilePortrait needs (e.g. border/reflection padding, align_corners variants), or must additional Metal kernel variants be written and validated against PyTorch?

What are the actual M3 Max (not M1 Max) forward+backward grid_sample throughput numbers, and is the resulting end-to-end MobilePortrait pipeline fast enough for the real-time/20fps target — i.e., does the GPU warping path remove the bottleneck or just shift it elsewhere?

For CoreML inference deployment, does a converted MobilePortrait (FOMM-style) model keep acceptable numerical accuracy (given the reported FP16 resample discrepancy, issue #2068) and does the resample op actually run on GPU/ANE rather than CPU for this model's specific tensor shapes?

Is it worth investing in a native PyTorch MPS custom grid_sample backward (using MetalShaderLibrary + autograd.Function) to keep an existing PyTorch training codebase, or is a full MLX rewrite of the warping core strictly the lower-effort path given MLX already ships the exact kernels?

refuted.claim: The grid_sampler_2d CPU-fallback / warning issue was resolved by upgrading to torch 2.1.0, and a PyTorch collaborator confirmed it no longer reproduces on torch 2.5.1 (issue closed Jan 2025).

The custom Metal grid_sample kernel produced an approximately 28x speedup during training versus the pure-MLX indexing implementation, demonstrating that the mx.fast.metal_kernel path delivers real GPU compute for warping architectures.

PR #125550 does NOT add the user-facing torch.mps.compile_shader runtime kernel-compilation API; it only introduces the internal C++ MetalShaderLibrary convenience class, and the actual custom-kernel infrastructure came in a later PR (#138636) built on this foundation.
